corrected_recommendation:
Re-verdict from "works-native-fast" to "works-native, latency budget unproven." The source work is unusually honest and the sources are real — this is not a hallucinated report — but its headline number is measured on an idle GPU and does not survive the system it is proposed for.

Keep, unchanged: Silero VAD v5 ONNX on CPU (but pull it from the official `snakers4/silero-vad`, not the `runanywhere` mirror — upstream's Python wrapper already handles the 64-sample context that caused the reported footgun), and SmartTurn v3.2-cpu ONNX on CPU with 4 intra-op threads. Both are CPU-only, cost under 2% of one core, and are therefore immune to the Metal contention that breaks the rest of the design. The two-stage endpointing argument (200 ms hangover instead of 600-800 ms) is the strongest surviving part of the report.

Change the ASR decision: do NOT commit to Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on the strength of the presented evidence. Make Qwen3-ASR-0.6B the default and treat Parakeet-TDT-0.6b-v3 as a live contender, because under realistic GPU load the 1.7B's cost is not the reported "130-234 ms per turn" but 400-750 ms per turn, which is a quarter to a third of the entire 2.0 s budget.

Gate the choice on two experiments the report itself proposes but does not run, and which must run before any model is picked, not after:
1. A CONTENDED bake-off. Load the intended local LLM and TTS, keep them resident and generating, and only then measure ASR p50/p90. Component-alone numbers are not admissible for a budget claim.
2. A REAL accented-speech set. Every number in the report comes from macOS `say` synthetic audio. Record 20-30 utterances of the user actually arguing, hand-transcribe, and run 1.7B / 0.6B / Parakeet. This is the only thing that settles whether Qwen's accent advantage is real for this speaker, and it is also the only valid way to measure SmartTurn's false-cut rate, which is meaningless on synthetic speech.

Budget the requirement properly: the stated hard requirement is user-stops-speaking to FIRST AUDIO OUT under ~2 s with barge-in. The report only measures to "transcript in hand" and does arithmetic on an assumed remainder. Instrument the full loop end to end before accepting any component. Note that the reference implementation this draws on measured ~1.9 s for SHORT sentences on a dedicated 4090 with the LLM in the cloud (ref-VoxEMW README line 91) and ~3.2 s for its full configuration (docs/plan-4090.md:178) — an all-local build on one shared Metal device is strictly harder than either.

Treat the ANE path as the fix, not an optimization. Since GPU contention is the measured failure mode, moving ASR off Metal entirely (FluidAudio / Parakeet-EOU on the Neural Engine, which also collapses VAD + SmartTurn + ASR into one model) addresses the actual bottleneck rather than shaving milliseconds off the wrong stage. Benchmark it before committing to a Python architecture. Also evaluate a duplex/streaming-native speech-to-speech design, which the report never considers and which removes the serial ASR-LLM-TTS stack that is the real source of the latency problem.

Plan for barge-in explicitly. The recommended three models cannot do it: the two-tier gate needs a fast interim transcript while the AI is speaking, which an offline Qwen pass cannot produce and which the report's own testing shows the streaming path corrupts. Budget a fourth concurrent model (Parakeet as the interim/interrupt transcriber) into memory, latency AND contention from the start.

problems.problem: FATAL — The end-to-end latency budget, the headline claim, is measured with an otherwise-idle GPU and collapses under the contention the final system guarantees. I reproduced this twice on this machine with a verified-live concurrent MLX workload (28-layer 4096x4096 fp16 matmul chain, itself far lighter than a real local LLM decode plus a TTS vocoder). The report lists GPU contention as a risk and an open question, then builds its verdict, its 611-934 ms figure, and its 'leaves 1.05-1.4 s for LLM TTFT + TTS TTFA' arithmetic on the uncontended number anyway. That is the classic error of presenting a component measurement as a system budget.
problems.evidence: Idle (my replication of their bench_final.py, matching their numbers): 1.4s clip p50 85.8 ms, 3.9s 315.0, 6.3s 435.3, 8.9s 673.5; active mem 4.08 GB / peak 8.16 GB exactly as claimed. Under one contender (two independent runs, contender confirmed alive at 248->200 steps/s, i.e. bidirectional contention): 1.4s p50 224.8 / 222.2 ms (2.6x), 3.9s 488.9 / 513.0 (1.6x), 6.3s 604.3 / 662.1 (1.4x), 8.9s 1180.1 / 1201.6 (1.8x); p90 on the 8.9s clip 2059.5 ms vs 782.6 idle (2.6x). Recomputing their own formula (200 ms hangover + ~50 ms endpoint + ASR) under contention: 3.9s utterance = 763 ms p50 / 915 ms p90; 6.3s = 912 ms p50; 8.9s = 1452 ms p50 and 2310 ms p90 — the hearing stack alone exceeds the entire 2.0 s target before the LLM sees a token. Raw logs: .cache/research and bench_contended2.log.

problems.problem: FATAL — Barge-in is an explicit hard requirement and the three recommended models cannot deliver it. The report's own barge-in design (duck TTS on VAD speech_start, commit to interrupt only once an ASR partial clears a word gate) requires a fast interim transcript WHILE the AI is speaking. An offline Qwen pass over a VAD-delimited buffer cannot produce one, and the report itself demonstrates that mlx-qwen3-asr's streaming path returns corrupted text and blocks the caller up to 1151 ms. So the design silently requires a fourth concurrently-resident model (Parakeet) that appears nowhere in the recommendation, the 4.1 GB memory total, the latency budget, or the contention analysis — and which makes problem #1 strictly worse.
problems.evidence: The recommendation names exactly three models and totals '~4.1 GB resident, ~8.2 GB peak.' Its own risk #9 concedes: 'you need a fast interim transcript during the AI's speech, which is the one place Parakeet's ~70 ms or a streaming model genuinely earns its keep.' Its own risk #4 rules out the streaming path: seam duplications in both finalization modes, 'feed_audio() also blocks up to 1151 ms on chunk boundaries, so it cannot live on the audio callback thread.' I confirmed the streaming API surface exists as described (init_streaming / feed_audio / finish_streaming, UNFIXED_CHUNK_NUM, UNFIXED_TOKEN_NUM, and a detect_repetition helper — the presence of a repetition detector in the module corroborates that seam artifacts are a known defect).

problems.problem: FATAL — The stated requirement is 'user stops speaking to FIRST AUDIO OUT under ~2 s', and the report never measures or bounds it. It measures only to 'transcript in hand' and then performs arithmetic on an assumed remainder for LLM TTFT + TTS TTFA. The reference implementation it draws on achieved its comparable number only with a dedicated 4090 AND the LLM offloaded to a cloud API — a strictly easier configuration than the proposed all-local single-Metal-device build.
problems.evidence: ./ref-VoxEMW/README.md line 91 measures '短句首音 ~1.9s' (short-sentence first audio ~1.9 s) on a 4090 with DeepSeek v4-flash via API and thinking disabled; the headline promises '说完 ~3s 开口' (~3 s to speak after you finish); docs/plan-4090.md:178 records '开口 ~3.2s' for the full configuration and :44 budgets 'STT 0.3~0.5s + DeepSeek ~0.6s + VoxCPM2 TTFA ~0.3~0.5s + SoulX 首帧 ~0.3s ≈ 1.5~2.2s'. Separately, configs/assistant.yaml:59 records a measured Mac-specific failure: '别升：实测 TTFA 翻倍且生成跟不上播放（内存带宽 2.6x）' — on the Mac path TTS generation already cannot keep ahead of playback due to memory bandwidth, before a 4.08 GB fp16 ASR model and a local LLM are added to the same device.

problems.problem: MAJOR — The single most consequential decision in the report (pay 4-8x the latency for Qwen over Parakeet) rests on one vendor's self-reported score on a private, unreleased internal test set, graded 'strong'. The numbers are real and I verified them, but 'Dialog-Accented English' is Qwen's own internal eval, not public, not reproducible, and has no independent corroboration. Meanwhile the counter-evidence that would close off the 4-8x faster model is graded 'weak-inference' by the author's own admission. Strong evidence for the preferred option and weak evidence against the alternative is not a decision — it is a preference with citations.
problems.evidence: Verified real at https://arxiv.org/html/2601.21337v1 Table 4: Qwen3-ASR-1.7B 16.07, 0.6B 16.62, Whisper-large-v3 21.30, GPT-4o-Transcribe 28.56, 'averaged over 16 accents'. But the paper's accented row contains NO Parakeet entry at all — the report concedes this — so the accent comparison that decides the recommendation never actually compares the two models in contention. The report's own note undercuts its recommendation: on this metric 1.7B beats 0.6B by only 0.55 pp (16.07 vs 16.62), which does not justify the 1.5-2.6x contended latency penalty measured above.

problems.problem: MAJOR — Source-attribution defect on the one piece of evidence that rejects the 4-8x faster alternative. The claim 'Parakeet degrades on L2-accented English' cites source_url https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3 and presents 'Published accent breakdown' with Japanese 9.74% / Russian 7.81%. I fetched that card: those numbers are not on it. The report does disclose in open_questions that the figure 'comes from a third-party study, not NVIDIA', but the evidence block still points the reader at an NVIDIA URL that does not support the quote.
problems.evidence: WebFetch of https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3 returned: 'The document does not report accent-specific WER metrics like Japanese-accented (9.74%) or Russian-accented (7.81%) performance. It provides language-level metrics instead.' The other figures attributed to that card DO check out (6.34% average WER clean, 11.66% at 0 dB SNR, CC-BY-4.0, 25 European languages), which makes the one unsupported quote the load-bearing one.

problems.problem: MAJOR — Every measurement in the report is on macOS `say` synthetic speech, which invalidates two different conclusions. (a) ASR latency: an autoregressive decoder's cost scales with output tokens, and synthetic speech is verbatim-clean; spontaneous L2 argument speech with disfluencies, restarts and filled pauses yields more tokens and more decoder uncertainty, so the numbers are optimistic, not 'pessimistic' as claimed. (b) Endpointing: SmartTurn's job is to classify hesitation patterns, and synthetic TTS has none — so the 200 ms hangover policy, which the report calls 'the single biggest latency lever in this component', is entirely unvalidated for the actual use case.
problems.evidence: Source clips are .aiff (macOS `say` default output) converted to wav in scratchpad/audio/: u3 1.400s, u2 3.892s, u1 6.347s, u4 8.944s — durations match the report's 1.4/3.9/6.3/8.9 exactly. Transcripts are fully fluent debate sentences with no disfluencies ('Look. The point I am making is that when you restrict access, you do not remove the demand...'). The report concedes the point in open_questions ('Every number in this report is from public benchmarks or from macOS `say` synthetic speech') yet still issues verdict 'works-native-fast' and a definitive model choice on that basis.

problems.problem: MINOR — The Silero VAD timing figures are not reproducible; I measure 2.6x the claimed mean and 5.7x the claimed p95. The conclusion (VAD compute is negligible) survives comfortably, but it shows the reported percentiles throughout are load-sensitive point estimates presented as stable measurements.
problems.evidence: Claimed: 0.139 ms mean / 0.215 ms p95 per frame. Measured on this machine, same file, same provider, correct 576-sample input, N=500: mean 0.363 ms, p95 1.224 ms. Still only ~1.1% of one core at a 32 ms frame rate, so the design conclusion is unaffected.

problems.problem: MINOR — Supply chain: the report recommends the unofficial third-party mirror `runanywhere/silero-vad-v5` for an always-on component, when the upstream `snakers4/silero-vad` exists and ships a maintained Python wrapper that already handles the 64-sample context correctly. The mirror is the direct cause of the silent-failure footgun the report had to discover by hand — it strips the wrapper and leaves the bare ONNX graph.
problems.evidence: The report's own text: 'The runanywhere README documents none of this.' The gotcha exists only because the raw ONNX graph accepts a dynamic [B,N] input and silently returns ~0.001 on a bare 512-sample frame; upstream's OnnxWrapper maintains the 64-sample context internally and never exposes the failure mode.

problems.problem: MINOR — Missed options, and one mis-prioritized. The report identifies FluidAudio's ANE path but files it as an optional 'optimization'; given that GPU contention is the empirically measured failure mode (problem #1), moving ASR off Metal is the direct fix for the actual bottleneck, not a nice-to-have. Separately, the report never evaluates a duplex or streaming-native speech-to-speech architecture at all, which would remove the serial ASR-LLM-TTS stack that is the real source of the latency problem for a barge-in-capable debate partner.
problems.evidence: The report's own alternatives entry concedes the point and then under-weights it: 'the architectural win (ASR off the GPU entirely) is larger than any per-model latency difference in this whole report' — yet the recommendation still selects the Metal-resident 4.08 GB fp16 model. The independent M5 Pro benchmark it cites (soniqo.audio/benchmarks, which I verified exists) also lists Parakeet-EOU at 232 MB doing streaming transcription with end-of-utterance built in, and a FireRedVAD row at 99.12 F1 on FLEURS that is never considered against Silero.

surviving_claims: The Qwen3-ASR Technical Report is real and correctly quoted. arXiv 2601.21337 exists, is titled 'Qwen3-ASR Technical Report', and Table 4 'Dialog-Accented English' contains exactly the claimed rows: Qwen3-ASR-1.7B 16.07, Qwen3-ASR-0.6B 16.62, Whisper-large-v3 21.30, GPT-4o-Transcribe 28.56, averaged over 16 accents. No fabrication. (The separate criticism is that this is a vendor's private eval set, not that it was misread.)

The smart-turn-v3 checkpoint claims are exactly right. I read the locally downloaded benchmarks/smart-turn-v3.2-cpu.md: 31,527 samples, 23 languages, generated 2026-01-07, English row n=7,820 at 94.26% accuracy / 3.75% FPR / 1.99% FNR. All five checkpoints ship as claimed, smart-turn-v3.2-cpu.onnx exists, license BSD-2.

The Pipecat two-stage endpointing defaults are quoted correctly: recommended VAD stop_secs 0.2 s ('which is the default value'), analyzer stop_secs default 3.0 s as the give-up timer, pre_speech_ms 500.0, max_duration_secs 8.0. Verified against docs.pipecat.ai.

The Silero VAD 512-vs-576-sample silent failure is REAL, SEVERE, and fully reproduced — this is the most valuable operational finding in the report. Feeding a bare 512-sample frame runs without error and returns near-zero probability on loud speech. My measurement on audio/u2.wav: bare 512 gives max prob 0.0567, mean 0.0014, 0/121 frames above 0.5; with the previous frame's last 64 samples prepended (576 total) it gives max 1.0000, mean 0.9908, 120/121 frames above 0.5. Total, undetectable failure exactly as described.

The '-hf' weight-layout trap is real and the corroboration is verbatim. mlx_qwen3_asr/convert.py in the installed package contains, at lines 13-16, 'Strip thinker. prefix from all keys / HF: thinker.audio_tower.conv2d1.weight -> audio_tower.conv2d1.weight', and the stripping logic at lines 29-33. The report verified this structurally rather than trusting the reference author's note, which is the right method.

The idle latency and memory measurements are honest and reproducible. My independent re-run of their bench_final.py produced p50 85.8 / 315.0 / 435.3 / 673.5 ms against their claimed 90 / 321 / 413 / 694 ms, and mx.get_active_memory() 4.08 GB / mx.get_peak_memory() 8.16 GB matching exactly. The methodology (in-memory float32 numpy, file I/O excluded, warm model, N=20) is sound. The numbers are not hand-waved — they are simply measured under the wrong conditions.

There is NO CUDA-only kernel trap on this path, and the report is right to have avoided one. This was the most likely place for the recommendation to break and it does not. mlx-qwen3-asr is genuinely torch-free; I confirmed mlx 0.32.2 and onnxruntime 1.29.0 CPUExecutionProvider installed and running natively in .venv-asr with no flash-attn, Triton, bitsandbytes, xformers, DeepSpeed or vLLM anywhere in the dependency graph. The report explicitly steers away from the vLLM deployment path on the Qwen model card, which would have been CUDA-only. The CoreML-EP-is-3x-worse finding for SmartTurn (graph shredded into 43 partitions) is the correct call and the corollary — that the reference repo's _patch_smart_turn_gpu monkeypatch is dead code on Mac — is right.
The Parakeet-TDT-0.6b-v3 model card facts are correct: 6.34% average WER clean, 11.66% at 0 dB SNR, CC-BY-4.0, 25 European languages. Only the accent-specific breakdown is mis-sourced.

The two-stage endpointing architecture is sound and is the strongest design argument in the report. Using SmartTurn to permit a 200 ms VAD hangover instead of 600-800 ms saves 400-600 ms on every turn for ~18 ms of CPU classification plus under 2% of one core for VAD. Both components are CPU-only and therefore immune to the Metal contention that breaks the ASR budget — which is precisely why they should be kept while the ASR choice is reopened.

The machine is as described: system_profiler confirms Apple M5 Max, 18 cores, 128 GB, macOS 26.5.2 build 25F84. Memory genuinely is a non-issue for this stack — the 16 GB constraint that forced the reference author onto the 0.6B does not transfer. (But memory was never the binding constraint; GPU contention is.)

The hotword hallucination analysis is mechanistically correct and the recommendation to use ZERO hotwords for an English debate partner is right. Qwen3-ASR hotwords enter the decoder as system-prompt context, so a long list both raises the token prior and presents a fluent continuable sequence — structurally the documented Whisper initial_prompt pathology. The reference repo's measured 10-hotword whole-segment recitation event and its is_vocabulary_recitation() guard corroborate it.

The operational risk list is unusually good and should be kept in full regardless of which ASR model is chosen: cold start 11.8 s requires boot-time warmup; in-flight ASR for a superseded turn must carry a turn id and be abandoned, not awaited; interrupt handling must count samples actually PLAYED rather than fed, because TTS generates faster than real time and writing the un-heard reply back to context desynchronises the argument; AEC is necessary but not sufficient and needs a transcript-level echo guard behind it; raw VAD speech-start is too trigger-happy for backchannel-dense debate and needs a word-count gate. These are all correct and hard-won.
